items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the criminal procedure law, the penal law and the executive
law, in relation to deed theft
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S6569

SPONSOR: MYRIE
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the criminal procedure law, the penal law and the execu-
tive law, in relation to deed theft

 
PURPOSE:

The purpose of this bill is to provide homeowners victimized by deed
theft with appropriate tools to fight evictions and recover property in
certain civil proceedings, and to makes other changes that strengthen
the ability of law enforcement officials to investigate, prosecute, and
take other remedial action against instances of deed theft.

 
SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section one of the bill would amend the Criminal Procedure Law to
increase the statute of limitations from five years to eight years only
with respect to the commission of a felony crimes related to a deed
theft or for fraud in connection with a real property transaction.

Sections two and three of the bill would amend the Penal Law to create
the new crime of deed theft and to clarify the penal law definition of
residential real property, which is referenced in the deed theft crime.

Section four of the bill would amend the Executive Law to provide the
Attorney General with concurrent jurisdiction to prosecute cases related
to deed theft and real estate related crimes.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Deed theft schemes rob families and communities of generational wealth.
Deed theft primarily occurs through forgery, where thieves falsify a
homeowner's signature without their knowledge, or through fraud, where
fraudsters deceive a homeowner into signing away title without realizing
what they have done. Deed thieves target mainly minority homeowners in
gentrifying neighborhoods with homes that have significantly appreciated
in value over the years, and that face some type of financial hardship,
like foreclosure, or tax or water liens.

The Office of the Attorney General (OAG), as chair of the Deed Theft
Task Force, regularly works with district attorneys' offices across the
state, local government, and legal services organizations to coordinate
our response to deed theft, discuss current trends in detecting, inves-
tigating and prosecuting deed theft, share research and analytics, and
exchange ideas on how to prosecute these complex crimes more effec-
tively. Based on the discussions of the Task Force and its own use of
both criminal and civil law to combat deed theft, the OAG is recommend-
ing to the Legislature the proposed amendments in this bill to aid its
work, those of other law enforcement partners, and to make it easier for
homeowners and civil practitioners to New York State Senate Memorandum
in Support of Legislation Submitted in accordance with Senate Rule VI,
Sec. 1 fend off attempted deed thefts and to restore title to their
property.  Often victims report deed theft too late because they learn
of the crime years later and prosecutors have no recourse but to close
the matter because the statute of limitations have run out.

Deed theft takes many forms and is often perpetrated by sophisticated
operations that take years to unwind. Often investigators find over time
that multiple properties have been stolen by the same perpetrators.
Investigating these crimes are thus resource and time intensive. Allow-
ing the OAG concurrent jurisdiction to investigate and prosecute these
crimes will provide relief and assist more victims. Current law does not
provide prosecutors or victims adequate tools and protections to combat
the various forms of deed theft. The new crime of deed theft will bring
awareness to this issue and send a message to deed thieves, as well as
law enforcement and the judiciary that the legislature will not tolerate
this crime. This bill includes broad but balanced solutions that will
protect those who have been victimized by deed theft and ensure that
such crimes are prosecuted.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New legislation.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

Undetermined. However, this bill would facilitate the ability of local
and state law enforcement to proceed with investigations and prose-
cutions in a more effective manner.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
30 days following enactment.

B.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S6569B

SPONSOR: MYRIE
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the criminal procedure law, the penal law and the execu-
tive law, in relation to deed theft

 
PURPOSE:

The purpose of this bill is to make changes that strengthen the ability
of law enforcement officials to investigate, prosecute, and take other
remedial action against instances of deed theft.

 
SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section one of the bill would amend the Criminal Procedure Law to set
the statute of limitations at five years after the commission of the
crime, or within two years of discovery of the facts constituting such
offense, with respect to the commission of a felony crime related to a
deed theft or for fraud in connection with a real property transaction.

Sections two and three of the bill would amend the crime of larceny
within the Penal Law to include deed theft as a specific form of larceny
and clarify the Penal Law definition of residential real property, which
is referenced in the language establishing deed theft as a form of
larceny.

Section four of the bill would amend the Executive Law to provide the
Attorney General with concurrent jurisdiction to prosecute cases related
to deed theft and real estate related crimes.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Deed theft schemes rob families and communities of generational wealth.
Deed theft primarily occurs through forgery, where thieves falsify a
homeowner's signature without their knowledge, or through fraud, when
fraudsters deceive a homeowner into signing away title without realizing
what they have done. Deed thieves target mainly minority homeowners in
gentrifying neighborhoods with homes that have significantly appreciated
in value over the years, and that face some type of financial hardship
like foreclosure or tax or water liens.  The addition to the penal law
will place a greater emphasis on the theft of someone's residence, rath-
er than value, and also emphasize the type of vulnerable victims that
prosecutors often see.

The Office of the Attorney General (OAG), as chair of the Deed Theft
Task Force, regularly works with district attorneys' offices across the
state, local government, and legal services organizations to coordinate
our response to deed theft, discuss current trends in detecting, inves-
tigating and prosecuting deed theft, share research and analytics, and
exchange ideas on how to prosecute these complex crimes more effec-
tively. Based on the discussions of the Task Force and its own use of
both criminal and civil law to combat deed theft, the OAG is recommend-
ing to the Legislature the proposed amendments in this bill to aid its
work, those of other law enforcement partners, and to make it easier for
homeowners and civil practitioners to fend off attempted deed thefts and
to restore title to their property.  Often victims report deed theft too
late because they learn of the crime years later and prosecutors have no
recourse but to close the matter because the statute of limitations have
run out. Nothing in this bill will preclude prosecutors from charging
deed thieves under other theories of larceny or other crimes, should
they deem it more appropriate.

Deed theft takes many forms and is often perpetrated by sophisticated
and organized fraudsters through schemes that sometimes take years to
unwind. Often investigators find over time that multiple properties have
been stolen by the same deed thieves. Deed thieves also improperly use
court proceedings like quiet title actions to effectuate the thefts of
homes from their rightful owners. Many of the victims of deed theft do
not have the financial resources to hire an attorney and contest the
fraudulent quiet title actions filed by the deed thieves. Investigating
these crimes are resource and time intensive. Allowing the OAG concur-
rent jurisdiction to investigate and prosecute these crimes will provide
relief and assist more victims. Current law does not provide prosecutors
or victims adequate tools and protections to combat the various forms of
deed theft. The clarification with regards to the crime of deed theft
will bring awareness to this issue, place more emphasis on the harmful
nature of stealing a residential home, and send a message to deed
thieves, as well as law enforcement and the judiciary that the legisla-
ture will not tolerate this crime. This bill includes broad but balanced
solutions that will protect those who have be en victimized by deed
theft and ensure that such crimes are prosecuted.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New legislation.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

Undetermined. However, this bill would facilitate the ability of local
and state law enforcement to proceed with investigations and prose-
cutions in a more effective manner.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
30 days following enactment.

summary: Relates to the theft of real property; defines certain larceny crimes as involving deed theft; authorizes the attorney general to investigate and prosecute every person or entity charged with the commission of a criminal offense in violation or transactions relating to deed theft or a transaction involving real property.
